explanations.explanation: That's it. When the disciples saw the babies coming, they rebuked the people who brought them (Luke 18:15). The text doesn't say why, so I'm not going to guess for them. I think those folks hoped for a warm welcome and got a stern word instead. Bringing a baby to Jesus and hearing a rebuke is a rough turn.
A line isn't what the disciples do, friend. Verse 15 says they rebuked the people who brought the babies. A rebuke is a firm word, and it's not a line-forming move.

Placing His hands on the babies is what the people wanted, since they were bringing the babies for Jesus to do that. What the disciples do, according to verse 15, is rebuke the people who brought them. Then Jesus is the one who calls the children to Him (Luke 18:16).

True, and Jesus says it plainly: “Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these.” He calls the children to Him first, and then He speaks. That's a welcome with the door held wide open.

This one is actually true, friend. Jesus says, “Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these.” So He tells them not to hinder the children, and He gives the kingdom of God as the reason. Easy one to second-guess, but He means it.

Yes! Jesus says, “Truly I tell you, anyone who does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it.” He says it right after He welcomes the children. Sometimes I think the lesson is in how a little one receives, and I'm still learning it myself. I've got a mustache full of flour and a lot to learn.

Faithful servant sounds like a nice one, but it's not the picture Jesus uses. He says, “Truly I tell you, anyone who does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it.” The children were right there, since He had just called them to Him. The picture He picks is a little child.

That's not the picture Jesus gives here. He says, “Truly I tell you, anyone who does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it.” The picture He uses is a little child, and the children are the ones He just called over to Him.

True. Jesus says, “No one is good except God alone.” He answers with a question first: “Why do you call Me good?” I won't guess what's behind it, because the text doesn't say. It just tells us what He says, and that's plenty to chew on.
This one is true, friend. Jesus replies, “Why do you call Me good?” and then says, “No one is good except God alone.” That's the text, word for word. Short answer, big weight.

Not quite, friend. After Jesus lists the commandments, the ruler says, “All these I have kept from my youth…” He doesn't mention breaking a single one. So the ruler's own words say the opposite of this card.
Right, it's false. The ruler answers, “All these I have kept from my youth…” That's his whole reply to the list. No confession of any slip-ups, just that he has kept them since he was young.

That's the one. Jesus says, “Sell everything you own and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven.” Notice He tells the ruler what he will have, not only what he gives up. I got bought for 25 cents at a bakery that was closing, and I can tell you treasure in heaven beats that any day.

Honor sounds like a good thing to get, but Jesus doesn't promise it here. He says, “Sell everything you own and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven.” The promise is treasure in heaven. People clapping isn't mentioned.

Peace in the house would be lovely, friend, but that's not what Jesus says. He says, “Sell everything you own and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven.” What the ruler will have is treasure in heaven, and that's the whole promise.
Yes. Jesus says, “Then come, follow Me.” Look at the order. First the selling and giving, then the following. The invitation to follow is the last thing He says to the ruler.
Teaching his town isn't what Jesus asks. After the selling and giving, He says, “Then come, follow Me.” The invitation is to come along with Him. No classroom is mentioned.
Staying put is the opposite of what Jesus says. His words are, “Then come, follow Me.” The ruler is invited to come along with Jesus. That's a different kind of road than the one he came in on.
That's what the text says: when the ruler heard it, he became very sad. I think this part hurts a little. The ruler asked a real question and got a real answer. Verse 24 says Jesus saw his sadness.

The text doesn't show the ruler arguing. It says he became very sad when he heard what Jesus told him. I think this is a quiet, heavy moment, not a loud one. No back-and-forth is recorded, just the sadness.

explanations.answer: He runs off to sell it
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, friend. It says he became very sad when he heard it. Nothing in verse 23 shows him running off to sell anything. I think this is one of the heavier moments in the passage, so I'll just stay with what's written.

Wealthy is right. Verse 23 says the ruler became very sad because he was extremely wealthy. That's the reason the text gives, so we can say it with confidence. I'll leave the rest of his heart to God.

Tired isn't what the verse says, friend. The ruler became very sad because he was extremely wealthy, and that's the reason the text gives. Tired is an easy guess, since sad and tired often show up together. But here the sadness is tied to his wealth, right after Jesus tells him to sell everything he owns.

Afraid is an easy guess, friend, because fear and sadness can look alike on a face. But the verse ties his sadness to one thing: he was extremely wealthy. That comes right after Jesus tells him to sell everything he owns and give to the poor.

explanations.answer: A camel passing through the eye of a needle
explanations.explanation: Yes! Jesus says, “Indeed, it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.” A camel is a big animal and a needle's eye is a tiny hole. That picture gets the point across fast, and nobody needs a diagram.

explanations.answer: A mountain being thrown into the sea
explanations.explanation: A mountain is a big picture, but it's not the one Jesus uses here. He says, “Indeed, it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.” The picture is a camel and a needle. Tiny hole, huge animal.

explanations.answer: A city on a hill being hidden away
explanations.explanation: That's not in this scene, friend. Here Jesus says, “Indeed, it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.” He uses a camel and a needle's eye. No city, no hill, just a huge animal and a tiny hole.

True. Those who heard Jesus asked, “Who then can be saved?” It's a fair question after the camel and the needle. I think they were stunned. That's my guess, because the text just gives us the question.

This one is true, friend. Those who heard Jesus say it asked, “Who then can be saved?” That's verse 26, word for word. After a camel and a needle's eye, I'd have been asking it too, probably louder. And Jesus has an answer for them.

God, yes. Jesus says, “What is impossible with man is possible with God.” That's His answer to the question about who can be saved. I know what it's like to think a thing is over for good, because I spent years in the back of a junk drawer. Then God reached in and called me out.
Faith is a good word, friend, but it's not the one Jesus uses. He says, “What is impossible with man is possible with God.” The answer points to God Himself. He's the one who makes it possible.
Prayer isn't the word here. Jesus says, “What is impossible with man is possible with God.” That's the whole sentence, and it ends with God. Not a method, but the One Himself.
That's what Peter says. Peter, one of Jesus' disciples, says, “Look, we have left all we had to follow You.” He says all, not a little. He's telling Jesus the whole of it.
Half is not the number Peter gives. Peter, one of Jesus' disciples, says, “we have left all we had to follow You.” He says all, friend. Not half, not a portion.
Some is a smaller claim than the one Peter makes, friend. Peter, one of Jesus' disciples, says, “we have left all we had to follow You.” He says all, and he says it straight out to Jesus.

Not quite, friend. Jesus says they won't have to wait for everything. He says they will receive many times more in this age, and in the age to come, eternal life. So there's something for now and something for later.

Right, it's false. Jesus says anyone who has left home or family for the sake of the kingdom of God will receive many times more in this age. Then He adds that in the age to come, they will receive eternal life. So it's not all saved up for later.

That's it. Jesus says that in the age to come, they will receive eternal life. That's the big one. Notice He gives them something in this age too, but eternal life is what He names for the age to come.
Long life in the land isn't what Jesus says. For the age to come, He promises eternal life. That's a bigger gift than a long one. It never runs out.
A home in Jerusalem isn't in His words, friend. Jesus says that in the age to come, they will receive eternal life. Not a house, but life with no end.
